title: India Just Had Its Fifth-Driest June Since 1901 — and the Monsoon Forecast for July Isn't Much Better
excerpt: Rainfall in June was nearly 40% below average as El Niño conditions strengthened. Summer crop planting is down 23% year-on-year, and the weather department expects below-average rain through July. For NRI investors, the monsoon is now the single biggest variable for inflation, rural demand, and RBI rate policy in the second half of the year.
body:
India ended June with rainfall 39.8% below its long-period average — the fifth-driest June since records began in 1901 and the worst in over a decade. And the outlook for July, the wettest and most critical month of the monsoon season, is not encouraging: the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast rainfall below 94% of the long-period average, with El Niño expected to strengthen further in the coming months.

For a $4-trillion economy where roughly half of all farmland lacks irrigation and half the population depends on agriculture, the numbers carry consequences that ripple far beyond the farm gate — into inflation, consumption, corporate earnings, and central bank policy.

## What Went Wrong in June

IMD Director-General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra attributed the severe shortfall to a convergence of unfavourable factors. The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), a band of wind and cloud that circles the equator and drives moisture into the subcontinent, was in an unfavourable phase for most of the month. No low-pressure system formed over the Bay of Bengal in June — a rarity, since the month typically sees two to three. And El Niño conditions, marked by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central Pacific, emerged during the month and suppressed monsoon activity.

The deficit worsened as the month progressed. By mid-June, rainfall was 32% below average. By June 21, the gap had widened to 41%, and it held there through the end of the month. An analysis of 36 states and union territories shows that only seven, covering just 21% of the country's total area, received normal or above-normal rainfall.

## Crop Planting Is Already Behind

The immediate impact is visible in the fields. Farmers have sown summer crops on just 18.27 million hectares as of June 25, nearly 23% less than the same date last year, according to the Ministry of Agriculture. The delays are concentrated in the crops that matter most:

- **Rice**: 2.58 million hectares planted, down from 3.44 million last year. India is the world's largest rice exporter, supplying about 40% of global shipments.
- **Soybeans**: 692,000 hectares, down a staggering 65% year-on-year.
- **Cotton**: 2.97 million hectares, down 35%.
- **Corn**: 1.57 million hectares, down 16%.

Sugar cane, which relies more on irrigation, was the sole bright spot, up 1.2%.

There is still time — July and early August are the critical sowing window, and farmers can make up significant ground if rains revive. Government warehouses also hold record-high rice stocks, up 15% from a year ago, which provides a buffer against a worst-case supply shock. But if July rainfall comes in as forecast — below average — the window for a full recovery narrows sharply.

## The Inflation Equation

India's retail inflation stood at 3.48% in April, comfortably below the Reserve Bank of India's 4% target. But food prices are the swing factor, and they are acutely sensitive to monsoon outcomes.

The Finance Ministry's monthly economic report, released Tuesday, acknowledged the risk: "Middle East conflict and below-normal monsoon rainfall underscore the need to rethink India's agricultural pricing policies." It noted that easing global commodity prices, including crude oil and urea, could help contain imported inflation, but flagged the monsoon as a domestic wildcard.

Bloomberg Economics projects inflation could reach 5.8% this fiscal year if monsoon rains remain below normal. In 2023, when rainfall was 5.4% below average, crop production fell 3.5% and food inflation surged to 8%. The current deficit is far larger.

"The confluence of elevated global energy prices, a depreciating rupee, rising upstream cost pressures, and the prospect of a below-normal monsoon calls for sustained policy vigilance," the Finance Ministry said.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

The monsoon is the most important macroeconomic variable in India for the second half of 2026. Here is what it affects:

**RBI rate path.** The central bank cut rates earlier this year as inflation fell, but Bloomberg Economics warns that "a poor monsoon season could increase the chances of a pivot to tightening." If food inflation spikes, the window for further easing closes. Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta has said the RBI's projections already factor in a 7-9% rainfall deficit — but a 40% June shortfall far exceeds that assumption.

**Rural consumption.** Weak monsoons hit rural incomes, which in turn drag on demand for two-wheelers, entry-level cars, tractors, FMCG products, and consumer durables. The auto index fell 2.1% on Monday on monsoon worries alone. Anand Rathi Research noted that "rural recovery and monsoon are the key monitorables" for FMCG sector growth this quarter.

**Food exports.** After the 2023 monsoon shortfall, India banned rice exports to stabilize domestic prices, disrupting a global trade that depends on India for 40% of supply. Analysts widely expect similar restrictions on sugar if this year's monsoon disappoints. NRI families who send money home may see purchasing power eroded if food inflation takes hold.

**Sector positioning.** FMCG and consumer staples companies with high rural exposure — Hindustan Unilever, Dabur, Marico, Britannia — are most vulnerable to a demand slowdown. Pharma, IT services, and companies with dollar-denominated revenues are relatively insulated. Irrigation and water infrastructure plays could see a policy tailwind.

The next two to three weeks of July rainfall data will determine whether the deficit narrows to manageable levels or deepens into a genuine agricultural crisis. For investors with India exposure, the monsoon forecast deserves at least as much attention as the Fed.

*Sources: India Meteorological Department, Reuters, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare, Ministry of Finance (Monthly Economic Report, June 2026), Bloomberg Economics, Anand Rathi Research, The Hindu Business Line*
